title: Programming fundamentals
summary: What code is, and how a computer turns it into action.
explanation: Programming means writing step-by-step instructions, called source code, for a computer.
A compiler translates the whole program first, while an interpreter reads and runs it line by line.
A runtime is the environment that runs your program, such as Node.js or the Python interpreter.
illustration:
source code
  |-> compiler
  |     -> machine code
  |        -> runs
  |-> interpreter
        -> runs, line by line
illustrationCaption: Two routes from source code to a running program. A compiler translates everything into machine code first. An interpreter reads and runs it line by line. Either way, a runtime does the running.

javascript.code: console.log("Hello!");
javascript.caption: One line of source code. Node.js or your browser is the runtime that runs it.

python.code: print("Hello!")
python.caption: One line of source code. The Python interpreter is the runtime that runs it.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; come back any time to read it again.

title: Syntax and semantics
summary: How code is written versus what it means.
explanation: Syntax is the set of rules for how code must be written, like the grammar of a sentence.
Semantics is what the code means, which is what it actually does when it runs.
Code can follow the syntax perfectly and still do the wrong thing.
illustration:
syntax error:
  print("Hi"
  (a bracket is missing, so the
   code cannot even be read)

semantic mistake:
  4 + 6 / 2
  (readable, but it means 4 + 3,
   not (4 + 6) / 2)
illustrationCaption: Two different kinds of mistake. A syntax error breaks the grammar, so the computer cannot read the line. A semantic mistake is readable code that means something other than what you intended.

javascript.code:
console.log(4 + 6 / 2);
console.log((4 + 6) / 2);
javascript.caption: Both lines are valid syntax. They print 7 and 5, because the brackets change the meaning.

python.caption: Both lines are valid syntax. They print 7.0 and 5.0, because the brackets change the meaning.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; you can revisit it whenever it helps.

title: Variables and constants
summary: Give a value a name, then use it.
explanation: A variable is a name for a value.
Once a value has a name, you can use the name wherever you would use the value.
A constant is a name whose value should never change, such as a tax rate.
task: Change the number stored in score to 12, then print the stored number.
successMessage: You stored 12 in score and printed it. Lesson done; try a different value whenever you like.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, const score = 7 gives the number 7 the name score and stops the name from being reassigned. Use let for a variable that will change.
javascript.exampleCode:
const score = 7;
console.log(score);

python.note: In Python, score = 7 gives the number 7 the name score. Python has no const, so names in ALL_CAPS, like MAX_SCORE, mark constants by habit.
python.exampleCode:
score = 7
print(score)

title: Data types
summary: Numbers, text, true/false and nothing at all.
explanation: A data type says what kind of value you have: a whole number, a decimal number, text, true or false, or nothing at all (null).
The type decides what you can do with a value, because adding numbers works differently from joining text.
Some languages check types before running (static typing), while JavaScript and Python check while running (dynamic typing).
task: The last value, nickname, holds nothing yet. Give it the text "Adi" so the last thing printed is Adi.
successMessage: nickname is text now, so it printed Adi instead of nothing. Lesson done; try changing the other values too.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, null means "no value" on purpose, and whole numbers and decimals share one number type.

python.note: In Python, None means "no value" on purpose, and whole numbers (int) and decimals (float) are separate types.
python.exampleCode:
name = "Ada"
age = 12
height = 1.5
is_student = False
nickname = None
print(name, age, height, is_student, nickname)

title: Operators
summary: Do math, compare values and combine conditions.
explanation: Operators are symbols that work on values: arithmetic (+ - * / %), comparison (> < ==), logical (and, or, not), assignment (= and +=), and bitwise (& and |, which work on binary digits).
An expression such as 9 % 4 pairs an operator with its values, and % gives the remainder after dividing.
Multiplication and division happen before addition and subtraction, and brackets change the order.
task: Change the first line to print the sum of 4 and 6, and the second line to print the remainder when 17 is divided by 5.
successMessage: 4 + 6 is 10, and 17 % 5 leaves a remainder of 2. Lesson done; try the other operators too.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, console.log(9 % 4) prints 1, the remainder of 9 divided by 4. The logical operators are && (and), || (or) and ! (not).
javascript.exampleCode:
console.log(2 + 3);
console.log(9 % 4);

python.note: In Python, print(9 % 4) prints 1, the remainder of 9 divided by 4. The logical operators are the words and, or and not.
python.exampleCode:
print(2 + 3)
print(9 % 4)

title: Expressions and statements
summary: Pieces that produce a value, and pieces that do something.
explanation: An expression is code that produces a value, such as width * height.
A statement is a complete instruction that does something, such as storing a value or printing one.
Statements are often built from expressions, like storing the result of an expression in a variable.
task: Replace the 0 with an expression, so area holds the width times the height and the program prints 24.
successMessage: width * height is an expression, and storing it in area is a statement. It printed 24. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, a statement usually ends with a semicolon.

python.note: In Python, each statement normally sits on its own line.
python.exampleCode:
width = 6
height = 3
area = width * height
print(area)

title: Input and output
summary: Show results and read what someone gives you.
explanation: Output is what a program shows, and input is what it receives, such as text typed by a person.
Programs read input as text, so what arrives is always a string.
Printing the result is how a program answers.
task: The program reads a name. Make it print Hello, then the name, then an exclamation mark, such as Hello, Ada!
successMessage: Your program greeted each name it was given. Lesson done; input and output are in almost every program.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8") reads everything that was typed, and .trim() removes the extra line break.
javascript.exampleCode:
const name = require("fs").readFileSync(0, "utf8").trim();
console.log("Hello, " + name + "!");

python.note: In Python, input() reads one line of typed text.
python.exampleCode:
name = input()
print("Hello, " + name + "!")

title: Type conversion
summary: Turn text into numbers and back, on purpose.
explanation: Type conversion changes a value from one type to another, such as the text "5" into the number 5.
Implicit conversion happens automatically, while explicit conversion is when you ask for it with a function.
Input arrives as text, so numbers you read must be converted before you do math with them.
task: The program reads two numbers, but they arrive as text, so + joins them instead of adding. Convert them so it prints their sum.
successMessage: You converted the text to numbers before adding, so 3 and 4 made 7 and not 34. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, Number("5") turns text into a number.

python.note: In Python, int("5") turns text into a whole number.
python.exampleCode:
text = "5"
number = int(text)
print(number + 1)

title: Conditional statements
summary: Make your program choose between paths.
explanation: A condition is a check with a true or false answer, such as temperature > 20 (greater than 20).
if runs a block when its check is true, else if tries another check, and else runs when nothing matched.
A switch picks one path by comparing a value with several exact options.
task: Add one more check so a temperature above 30 prints Hot. Above 20 still prints Warm, and everything else prints Cool.
successMessage: Your three paths work: Hot, Warm and Cool. Lesson done; the order of the checks is what made it work.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, else if adds another check, and a switch statement compares a value with several case labels.

python.note: In Python, elif adds another check, and the indented lines under each check belong to it.

title: Loops and iteration
summary: Repeat work without repeating yourself.
explanation: A loop repeats code until a stopping rule says to finish.
A for loop counts through a range, a while loop runs as long as a condition stays true, and a do-while loop always runs once before checking.
break leaves a loop early, and continue skips straight to the next turn.
task: The loop prints 1 to 5. Change it so it skips 3 and prints 1, 2, 4 and 5, each on its own line.
successMessage: continue skipped the number 3 and the loop carried on with 4 and 5. Lesson done.

javascript.note: This for loop starts count at 1, continues while count <= 3 (at most 3), and adds 1 after each turn. A while or do...while loop does the same with just a condition.

python.note: In Python, range(1, 4) gives 1, 2 and 3: it starts at 1 and stops just before 4. Python has no do-while; a while loop with break does the same job.
python.exampleCode:
for count in range(1, 4):
    print(count)

title: Functions and procedures
summary: Package steps into a reusable, named tool.
explanation: A function is a named piece of code you can run whenever you need it.
A parameter is a name for a value the function receives, an argument is the value you pass in, and return sends a result back.
A function that only does something, without returning a value, is often called a procedure.
task: Make greet use its name parameter, so greet("Ada") returns "Hello, Ada!" and greet("Mia") returns "Hello, Mia!".
successMessage: greet now uses whatever name it is given. Lesson done; one function, many results.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, function add(first, second) { ... } defines the function, and add(2, 3) calls it with two arguments.

python.note: In Python, def add(first, second): defines the function, and add(2, 3) calls it with two arguments.

title: Scope and lifetime
summary: Where a name can be seen, and how long it lives.
explanation: Scope is the part of a program where a name can be used.
A local variable lives inside one function and disappears when the function ends, while a global variable can be seen everywhere.
Code can look outward at the names around it (lexical scope), but not inward at a function's locals.
task: This program crashes because message only exists inside makeMessage. Fix it so it prints Scope works!
successMessage: message lives inside the function, so the function returned it to the outside. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, const and let belong to the nearest pair of curly braces, and a function can read names from the code around it.

python.note: In Python, a name made inside def is local to that function, and a function can read names defined outside it.
python.exampleCode:
greeting = "Hello"

def shout():
    ending = "!"
    return greeting + ending

print(shout())

title: Mutability and immutability
summary: Values that can change, and values that can't.
explanation: A mutable value can be changed in place, while an immutable value never changes, and any "change" makes a new value.
Lists are mutable, and text strings are immutable.
Knowing which is which explains why a change can show up in more than one place.
task: Add "done" to the list tags, so the program prints 3 for the number of items.
successMessage: You changed the list in place, so it now holds three items. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, const stops the name from being reassigned, but the list itself is still mutable, so push can change it.

python.note: In Python, lists are mutable, so append changes the list itself, while strings and tuples never change.
python.exampleCode:
word = "cat"
loud = word.upper()
print(word, loud)

title: Error handling
summary: Expect things to go wrong, and recover calmly.
explanation: An error happens when something goes wrong while a program runs, such as turning the text "abc" into a number.
Validation checks input before it is used, and error handling lets a program recover instead of crashing.
A friendly message that says what to fix is better than a crash.
task: Right now bad input breaks the program. Make it print "Please enter a number" when the input is not a number, and print double the number otherwise.
successMessage: Good numbers are doubled and bad input gets a friendly message instead of a crash. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, Number("abc") does not crash; it gives NaN (not a number), which this practice runner shows as null, so check with Number.isNaN. Code that can throw is wrapped in try and catch.

python.note: In Python, int("abc") raises a ValueError. try runs the risky code, and except catches the error so the program can recover.

title: Arrays and lists
summary: Keep many values in order.
explanation: An array (a list in Python) keeps many values in order.
Each value has a position called an index, and the first index is 0.
You can read an item by its index, add items, and ask how many there are.
task: The program reads some numbers. Make it print the last number instead of the first.
successMessage: You found the last item, whatever the length of the list. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, fruits[1] reads the second item, and fruits.length tells how many items there are.
javascript.exampleCode:
const fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"];
console.log(fruits[1]);

python.note: In Python, fruits[1] reads the second item, len(fruits) tells how many items there are, and fruits[-1] is the last item.
python.exampleCode:
fruits = ["apple", "banana", "cherry"]
print(fruits[1])

title: Strings and text processing
summary: Search, slice and format text.
explanation: A string is text, and each character has an index just like an item in an array.
You can slice out a piece, search for text inside it, and format it, for example by changing the case.
Under the hood each character is stored as a number using an encoding such as Unicode.
task: The program reads a word. Make it print only the first three letters, in capital letters.
successMessage: You sliced the word and changed its case. Lesson done; text tools like these are everywhere.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, word.slice(0, 3) takes the first three characters, and word.toUpperCase() changes the case.
javascript.exampleCode:
const word = "banana";
console.log(word.slice(1, 4));

python.note: In Python, word[:3] takes the first three characters, and word.upper() changes the case.
python.exampleCode:
word = "banana"
print(word[1:4])

title: Stacks and queues
summary: Last in first out, and first in first out.
explanation: A stack is last in, first out, like a pile of plates where you take from the top.
A queue is first in, first out, like a line at a shop where you serve the front.
Both are lists with a rule about which end you add to and which end you take from.
task: The program takes words from the front, like a queue, so they print in the same order. Change it to take from the end, like a stack, so the words print in reverse.
successMessage: Taking from the end made it a stack, so the last word in came out first. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, push adds to the end, pop removes from the end, and shift removes from the front.

python.note: In Python, append adds to the end, pop() removes from the end, and pop(0) removes from the front.
python.exampleCode:
stack = []
stack.append("a")
stack.append("b")
print(stack.pop())

title: Maps and dictionaries
summary: Look things up by a key.
explanation: A map (a dictionary in Python, an object in JavaScript) stores values under keys, so you can look one up by name.
Looking up a key is fast, even when the map holds many items.
Counting is a classic use: each word is a key and its count is the value.
task: The program should count how many times each word appears, then print the count for apple. Right now every count stays at 1. Fix the counting.
successMessage: Each word now adds one to its own count. Lesson done; counting with a map shows up everywhere.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, counts[word] reads a key, and (counts[word] || 0) gives 0 when the key is missing.
javascript.exampleCode:
const ages = { Ada: 12, Mia: 9 };
console.log(ages["Mia"]);

python.note: In Python, counts.get(word, 0) gives 0 when the key is missing.
python.exampleCode:
ages = {"Ada": 12, "Mia": 9}
print(ages["Mia"])

title: Sets
summary: A collection with no duplicates.
explanation: A set holds values with no duplicates, and adding a value that is already there changes nothing.
Checking whether a value is in a set is fast.
Sets are handy for removing duplicates and for asking whether you have seen something before.
task: The program reads some numbers. Make it print how many different numbers there are, counting each value once.
successMessage: A set keeps each value once, so its size is the number of different values. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, new Set(numbers) removes duplicates, and its size property says how many values remain.
javascript.exampleCode:
const seen = new Set([1, 2, 2, 3]);
console.log(seen.size);

python.note: In Python, set(numbers) removes duplicates, and len(...) says how many values remain.
python.exampleCode:
seen = set([1, 2, 2, 3])
print(len(seen))

title: Linked lists
summary: Values chained together, one link at a time.
explanation: A linked list is a chain of nodes, and each node holds a value and a link to the next node.
The last node links to nothing (null or None), which is how you know the chain has ended.
To visit every node you start at the head and keep following the links.
task: The program builds a linked list from the words it reads but only prints the first one. Walk the chain by following next links, and print every value on its own line.
successMessage: You followed the links from the head until there were none left. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, a while loop that runs until current is null is the usual way to walk a chain.

python.note: In Python, a while loop that runs until current is None is the usual way to walk a chain.

title: Trees
summary: Hierarchies, and binary search trees.
explanation: A tree is a hierarchy with one root node at the top, and each node can have children below it.
In a binary tree each node has at most two children, called left and right.
In a binary search tree smaller values go left and larger values go right, so visiting left, then the node, then right gives the values in sorted order.
task: The program builds a binary search tree from the numbers it reads, but inOrder only prints the root. Make inOrder visit the left side first, then the node, then the right side, so the numbers print in sorted order.
successMessage: Left, node, right: the recursion walked the whole tree in sorted order. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, a function that calls itself on node.left and node.right walks the tree one branch at a time.

python.note: In Python, a function that calls itself on node.left and node.right walks the tree one branch at a time.

title: Graphs
summary: Nodes, edges and how to walk them.
explanation: A graph is a set of nodes joined by edges, such as people and friendships or cities and roads.
Traversal means visiting every node you can reach, and breadth-first search visits the nearest nodes first.
A visited set stops you from going round in circles.
task: The program starts a breadth-first walk from the node it reads, but never adds any neighbours to the queue. Add each neighbour that has not been visited yet, so every reachable node is printed.
successMessage: The queue visited the nearest nodes first, and the visited set kept D from printing twice. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, a Set remembers visited nodes, and an array used as a queue gives the order with push and shift.
javascript.exampleCode:
const graph = { A: ["B", "C"], B: ["D"], C: ["D"], D: [] };
console.log(graph["A"].join(" "));

python.note: In Python, a set remembers visited nodes, and a list used as a queue gives the order with append and pop(0).

title: Searching algorithms
summary: Linear and binary search.
explanation: Searching means finding where a value is, or finding out that it is missing.
Linear search checks items one by one, so it can take as many steps as there are items.
Binary search works on sorted data and halves the search area each step, so it needs only a handful of steps.
task: Finish the binary search. The program reads sorted numbers and a target, and prints the target's index or -1. In each branch, throw away the half that cannot hold the target.
successMessage: Each step threw away half of what was left. Lesson done; that is why binary search is so fast.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, Math.floor((low + high) / 2) finds the middle index, and low and high mark the part still being searched.
javascript.exampleCode:
const numbers = [4, 8, 15, 16];
console.log(numbers.indexOf(15));

python.note: In Python, (low + high) // 2 finds the middle index, and low and high mark the part still being searched.
python.exampleCode:
numbers = [4, 8, 15, 16]
print(numbers.index(15))

title: Sorting algorithms
summary: Bubble, insertion, merge and quick sort.
explanation: Sorting puts items in order, which makes searching and comparing much easier.
Bubble sort swaps neighbours that are out of order, and insertion sort slides each item into its place.
Merge sort and quicksort split the work into smaller parts, which is much faster on big lists.
task: This bubble sort compares neighbours but never swaps them. Add the swap so the numbers print in order, smallest first.
successMessage: Each pass pushed the biggest remaining number to the end, and the list came out sorted. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, swapping two items needs a temporary variable so neither value is lost.

python.note: In Python, a, b = b, a swaps two values in one line.
python.exampleCode:
numbers = [3, 1, 2]
numbers.sort()
print(" ".join(map(str, numbers)))

title: Recursion
summary: A function that solves a smaller version of itself.
explanation: Recursion means a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
Every recursive function needs a base case that stops the calls, and a recursive case that moves toward it.
Without a base case it would call itself forever.
task: factorial(n) multiplies n by every whole number below it, so factorial(5) is 120. The base case is done, but the recursive case just returns 0. Replace it with a call to factorial on a smaller number.
successMessage: Each call handled one number and left the rest to a smaller call. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, a function can call itself by name inside its own body.

python.note: In Python, a function can call itself by name inside its own body.

title: Algorithmic complexity
summary: Big O: how time and space grow with the input.
explanation: Big O describes how the time or memory a program needs grows as its input gets bigger.
O(1) stays the same, O(n) grows in step with the input, and O(n squared) grows much faster, such as a loop inside a loop.
Time is how many steps a program takes, and space is how much extra memory it uses.
illustration:
items       10    1,000    1 million
O(1)         1        1        1
O(log n)     4       10       20
O(n)        10    1,000    1 million
O(n^2)     100    1 million  too slow
illustrationCaption: How many steps each kind of growth needs as the input gets bigger. O(1) and O(log n) barely change, O(n) grows in step with the input, and O(n squared) quickly becomes far too slow.

javascript.caption: With three items, the single loop takes 3 steps and the nested loops take 9, 12 in all. With a thousand items it would be 1,000 and 1,000,000.

python.caption: With three items, the single loop takes 3 steps and the nested loops take 9, 12 in all. With a thousand items it would be 1,000 and 1,000,000.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; Big O gets easier the more programs you read.

title: Problem-solving techniques
summary: Decomposition, two pointers, sliding window, divide and conquer.
explanation: Problem-solving techniques are reusable ideas: decomposition splits a big problem into small steps, two pointers walk in from both ends, a sliding window moves over a range, and divide and conquer splits the data in half.
Most of them turn slow repeated work into a single careful pass.
Naming the technique helps you spot the same shape in a new problem.
task: Use two pointers to check whether any two different numbers in a sorted list add up to the target. Finish the two branches: move the left pointer up when the sum is too small, and the right pointer down when it is too big.
successMessage: Two pointers closed in from both ends and checked each pair once. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, two index variables, left and right, start at the ends and move toward each other.

python.note: In Python, two index variables, left and right, start at the ends and move toward each other.
python.exampleCode:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4]
left = 0
right = len(numbers) - 1
while left < right:
    print(numbers[left] + numbers[right])
    left += 1
    right -= 1

title: Abstraction
summary: Hide the details, keep the idea.
explanation: Abstraction means hiding the details and showing only what you need to use something.
You press a button on a microwave without knowing how it heats food, and a function works the same way.
Good abstractions let you think about what a piece of code does, not how it does it.
illustration:
you call:        average(list)
                    |
hidden inside:   add them up
                 count them
                 divide
illustrationCaption: The caller only sees the name average and what it returns. The adding, counting and dividing stay hidden inside the function.

javascript.caption: You use average without caring how it adds and divides.

python.caption: You use average without caring how it adds and divides.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; come back whenever you want a refresher.

title: Encapsulation
summary: Keep data and the code that guards it together.
explanation: Encapsulation keeps data and the code that works on it together, and controls how outsiders can reach it.
Other code uses a small set of methods instead of changing the data directly.
That way the data can be protected from invalid changes.
illustration:
+------------------------+
| Account                |
|   balance  (hidden)    |
|   deposit(amount)      |
|   get balance          |
+------------------------+
   only these are public
illustrationCaption: An Account object keeps its balance private. The outside can only use the methods the account offers, so every change goes through its checks.

javascript.caption: The # makes the balance private. deposit rejects the negative amount, so the balance stays 50.

python.caption: The leading underscore marks the balance as private by habit. deposit rejects the negative amount, so the balance stays 50.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; come back whenever you want a refresher.

title: Modularity
summary: Build programs from small, swappable parts.
explanation: Modularity means building a program from small, separate parts called modules, each with one clear purpose.
A module can be changed, tested or replaced without rewriting everything else.
Parts connect through a few clear entry points.
illustration:
main
 |-- input    (read the data)
 |-- rules    (decide)
 |-- output   (show the result)
illustrationCaption: A program split into three modules. Each one does a single job, and main joins them together.

javascript.caption: Three small functions, each with one job, joined in one line.

python.caption: Three small functions, each with one job, joined in one line.

successMessage: You got them all. Lesson done; come back whenever you want a refresher.

title: Object-oriented programming
summary: Classes, objects, inheritance, composition and polymorphism.
explanation: A class is a blueprint, and an object is one thing built from it, with its own data and behaviour.
Inheritance lets a class reuse another class's code, composition builds a class by holding other objects, and polymorphism lets different classes answer the same method call in their own way.
Use inheritance when something truly is a kind of something, and composition when it has something.
task: The program reads animal kinds and asks each one to speak. Cat does not have its own speak yet, so it prints ... Give Cat a speak method that returns Meow.
successMessage: Each class answered speak in its own way, and the loop did not need to know which was which. That is polymorphism. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, class Dog extends Animal inherits from Animal, and a method with the same name overrides it.

python.note: In Python, class Dog(Animal) inherits from Animal, and a method with the same name overrides it.

title: Functional programming
summary: Pure functions, higher-order functions and immutability.
explanation: A pure function always returns the same result for the same inputs and changes nothing outside itself.
A higher-order function takes a function as an argument or returns one, as map and filter do.
Building new values instead of changing old ones makes code easier to follow.
task: The program prints the square of every number. Change it so it only squares the even numbers, by filtering first and then mapping, and prints those squares.
successMessage: filter chose the even numbers and map squared them, with no loop and no changes to the original list. Lesson done.

javascript.note: In JavaScript, numbers.filter(test) keeps the items that pass, and numbers.map(change) builds a new list of results.

python.note: In Python, filter(test, numbers) keeps the items that pass, and map(change, numbers) builds the results.
python.exampleCode:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
doubled = list(map(lambda n: n * 2, numbers))
print(" ".join(map(str, doubled)))

title: Declarative vs imperative
summary: Say what you want, or say how to get it.
explanation: Imperative code spells out how to do something, step by step.
Declarative code states what result you want and lets the language or library work out the steps.
Most programs mix both styles.
illustration:
imperative:
  take a number, is it even?
  if yes, put it in a new list...

declarative:
  give me the even numbers
illustrationCaption: The same job described two ways. The imperative version lists every step, while the declarative version only says what is wanted.

title: Data integrity and transactions
summary: Constraints and ACID.
explanation: Data integrity means the data stays correct and consistent, which databases protect with constraints such as unique keys and required values.
A transaction groups several changes so they all succeed or all fail together.
ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability, the four promises a reliable transaction makes.
illustration:

  take 50 from Ada
  give 50 to Mia
COMMIT      all changes stick

an error?  ROLLBACK, nothing changed
illustrationCaption: A money transfer as a transaction. Either both steps happen and are committed, or an error undoes everything and the balances stay as they were.

python.code:
import sqlite3

db = sqlite3.connect(":memory:")
db.execute("CREATE TABLE accounts (name TEXT PRIMARY KEY, balance INTEGER CHECK (balance >= 0))")
db.execute("INSERT INTO accounts VALUES ('Ada', 100)")
db.commit()
try:
    with db:
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 30 WHERE name = 'Ada'")
        db.execute("UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 90 WHERE name = 'Ada'")
except sqlite3.IntegrityError:
    print("rolled back")
print(db.execute("SELECT balance FROM accounts").fetchone()[0])
python.caption: The second update breaks the CHECK constraint, so the whole transaction is rolled back, including the first update, and the balance is still 100.
